content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses converge on grace as God's unmerited, freely given favor toward undeserving sinners, supremely expressed in salvation through Christ (Eph 2:8-9; Rom 3:24; Titus 2:11). All list a common secondary sense of grace as divine empowering/transforming power that enables holy living (2 Cor 12:9; 1 Cor 15:10; Titus 2:11-12), plus tradition-specific mechanics (sacramental infusion, uncreated energies, chesed overlap, aesthetic charm).","book_summary":"Grace is favor that moves first (prior to any human merit, Rom 5:8) and then teaches its recipient to reject ungodliness and live rightly (Titus 2:11-12). The book insists the pedagogical, transformative function is constitutive of grace, and brands as 'counterfeit grace' any construal that treats favor as permission to remain lawless.","consensus_core_identification":"Grace = God's unmerited favor freely given to sinners, centered on salvation in Christ apart from works.","book_core_identification":"Grace = unmerited favor that initiates before merit AND necessarily continues as a teacher producing godly living; favor without the teaching function is not grace but its counterfeit.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUBSET","boundary_disagreement":"The book excludes from 'grace' any conception of unmerited favor detached from its sanctifying/teaching work — i.e., antinomian or 'license' readings that the bare consensus definition ('unmerited favor by which sinners are saved') could tolerate if stated without qualification. The consensus treats the empowering/training dimension as a common but secondary alternative; the book makes it a necessary condition of the term's true extension, reclassifying favor-as-permission as counterfeit rather than as a variant of grace.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"The book preserves the consensus's central referent: unmerited divine favor that moves first toward sinners (Rom 5:8 matches the consensus core exactly, and the book's own common-view note acknowledges this). Its change is at the boundary: it fuses the consensus's primary meaning with the widely listed secondary meaning (grace as transforming/training power, explicitly cited by Response C from Titus 2:11-12) and makes that fusion definitional, denying the name 'grace' to favor construed as tolerance of lawlessness. This is a material tightening of conditions, not a replacement of the referent, so REFINED rather than MATCH (the exclusion of permission-only grace is a real boundary claim) and not DIVERGENT (no consensus identification is contradicted; the consensus itself never affirms grace as license).","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue this is a MATCH: mainstream teaching also rejects antinomianism (e.g., Rom 6:1-2 is standard), and several consensus responses already list grace's training function (Titus 2:11-12 appears in Responses A, C, D), so the book may merely be foregrounding an accepted nuance rather than genuinely narrowing the term's extension.","confidence":"high"}
